title: Discriminated unions and switch exhaustiveness
hook: A discriminated union tags each variant with a shared literal field — kind, type, or status. Switch on that tag and TypeScript narrows each branch; the never exhaustiveness check catches missing cases when the API adds a variant.

blocks.text: A **discriminated union** (tagged union) is a union of object types sharing a **discriminant** property with a unique **literal type** per variant. Example: `type Result = { status: 'ok'; data: User } | { status: 'error'; message: string }`. When you `switch (result.status)`, each case narrows `result` to one variant — `data` exists only in the `'ok'` branch. **Exhaustiveness checking** uses `default: const _exhaustive: never = value` to force a compile error when a new variant is added but switch is not updated.

entries.plainDefinition: Shared field with a literal type unique per union member — usually kind, type, or status.
Compiler verifies every union member handled — often via never in default branch.
TypeScript refines union type in each branch based on discriminant comparison.
Bottom type — assignable to nothing; used when all cases handled.
entries.example: const x: never = value; // error if value not never

blocks.text: Redux actions, API event streams, payment state machines, and AST nodes all use discriminated unions. Without exhaustiveness, adding `{ status: 'pending' }` silently breaks a switch that only handled ok/error — runtime falls through, UI shows blank. C# has discriminated unions in C# 12 with `switch` expressions and required patterns; TypeScript does this at compile time only. Reddit senior threads rank exhaustiveness with `never` as a must-know pattern.

blocks.title: Discriminant must be readonly literal
blocks.body: Use status: 'ok' not status: string — widening to string breaks narrowing. as const on object literals helps.

blocks.title: Optional discriminant
blocks.body: If tag field is optional, union does not discriminate reliably — make tag required on every variant.

blocks.title: if/else chain without default never
blocks.body: Switch exhaustiveness is idiomatic — if-chains forget default never and miss new variants.

blocks.text: Combine with narrowing at boundaries: parse unknown to discriminated union after validation. Libraries like @reduxjs/toolkit use PayloadAction<T> pattern. Senior follow-up: distribute conditional types over unions (module 12). assertNever helper centralizes runtime throw for impossible cases in production logging. Pattern matching proposal may add native match — today switch + never is the idiomatic answer.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot define tagged union. No never exhaustiveness. Using string discriminant without literals. Saying TypeScript checks discriminant at runtime.

interviewTakeaways: Discriminated union = shared literal tag + variant-specific fields.
switch on tag narrows type per branch — IntelliSense knows fields.
default: const x: never = val — exhaustiveness when union grows.
60s: Tag with kind/type/status literal. Switch narrows. never in default catches missing cases. Runtime is plain JS objects. Pairs with API unknown narrowing.
Follow-up: combine with Zod discriminatedUnion or assertNever helper.
commonPitfalls: Weak: type: string discriminant — no narrowing.
Weak: no default never — new variant silent bug.
Strong: 'Literal tag per variant. Switch exhaustiveness with never. Validate unknown into union at boundary.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Redux actions { type, payload } are discriminated unions at runtime — TypeScript adds compile-time narrowing on switch.
Discriminated unions are a refined union pattern — requires literal discriminant for control-flow analysis.
